entities.summary:
Publius Calvisius Tullus Ruso was a Roman politician in the 2nd century AD, serving as the Praetorian Prefect from 161 to 162 AD and as the Consul in 145 AD. His significance lies in his role as a key figure in the Roman administrative reforms of the 2nd century AD, which aimed to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Roman state. During his tenure, he implemented various policies aimed at reducing corruption and increasing the power of the Roman Senate.

He played a crucial role in the Roman Empire's military campaigns in Dacia, leading the army to several victories against the Dacian king Decebalus. His success in these campaigns led to the expansion of the Roman Empire into the region, which had significant consequences for the cultural and economic development of the region.

Despite his significant contributions to the Roman Empire, Publius Calvisius Tullus Ruso's legacy is largely forgotten in modern historiography, with many historians viewing his role as that of a minor administrator. However, his impact on the Roman administrative reforms of the 2nd century AD remains an important area of study for historians seeking to understand the complexities of Roman governance.

The Roman historian Tacitus, in his work 'The Histories', describes Calvisius Ruso as a 'good and honest man' who was 'very skilled in the affairs of the state' and 'very experienced in the management of the public treasury'. This quote highlights the esteem in which he was held by his contemporaries and underscores the importance of his role in Roman politics.

Despite his relatively minor status in modern historiography, Publius Calvisius Tullus Ruso remains an important figure in understanding the complexities of Roman governance and the impact of the Roman administrative reforms of the 2nd century AD on the development of the Roman Empire.
